government.name: District of North Vancouver
government.howBuilt: This list draws on District of North Vancouver candidates' own platforms and campaign websites, local news coverage of candidate announcements, and public statements about the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant costs. We kept issues the District can act on through zoning, its budget, utility rates, local roads, parks, and its role at Metro Vancouver. Matters mainly run by the province or federal government, such as health care and school funding, are left out of this list.

issues.title: Housing growth and density
issues.description: How much new housing the District allows, what types, and where it goes, including town centres and existing single-family neighbourhoods.
issues.whatItAffects: Renters, first-time buyers, seniors looking to downsize, families, and residents of established neighbourhoods.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the Official Community Plan and zoning, approves rezonings and development permits, and sets development fees and amenity requirements within provincial housing rules.

viewQuestion.question: How should the District approach new housing?
viewQuestion.poleA: Allow more homes faster, including more density across neighbourhoods
viewQuestion.poleB: Grow more gradually and only where transit and services are in place

tradeoffs.context: Housing choices often trade how quickly new homes are built against how much neighbourhoods change and how fast services keep up.

gains: More homes could be built sooner, easing pressure on rents and prices
More people living locally may support shops, transit, and workers
costs: Traffic, schools, and pipes may come under more strain before upgrades arrive
Some neighbourhoods may see more change in height and character

gains: New homes may be better matched with transit, roads, and amenities
Existing neighbourhoods may keep more of their current scale and feel
costs: Fewer new homes could keep rents and prices higher for longer
Workers and young families may keep commuting in from elsewhere

issues.title: Traffic congestion and transit
issues.description: How the District tackles North Shore traffic, including local road changes, transit priority, cycling routes, and advocacy for a new Second Narrows crossing and rapid transit.
issues.whatItAffects: Commuters, transit riders, businesses, emergency response times, and people walking and cycling.
issues.whoDecides: Council controls District roads, lane use, and cycling and walking networks, and advocates to TransLink and the province on bridges, highways, and rapid transit.

viewQuestion.question: Where should the District focus its transportation efforts?
viewQuestion.poleA: Give more road space and priority to transit, walking, and cycling
viewQuestion.poleB: Focus on road and intersection changes that move vehicle traffic

tradeoffs.context: Road space and budgets are limited, so priority for one way of travelling can mean less room or money for another.

gains: More people could travel without adding cars to crowded roads
Transit and cycling options may lower travel costs for some households
costs: Drivers may face fewer lanes or slower trips on some streets
Major transit depends on regional and provincial funding the District does not control

gains: Drivers and trades may see quicker trips on key routes
Changes to local roads can often be made sooner and more directly
costs: Added road capacity may fill with new traffic over time
Less space or money may be left for transit and active travel

issues.title: Property taxes and District spending
issues.description: How much the District raises through property taxes and utility fees each year, and which services and projects that money pays for.
issues.whatItAffects: Homeowners, renters through their rent, businesses, and everyone who uses District services.
issues.whoDecides: Council adopts the annual budget and five-year financial plan, sets tax rates and utility fees, and decides which services and projects to fund or delay.

viewQuestion.question: How should the District balance its budget?
viewQuestion.poleA: Hold tax increases close to inflation, even if some projects wait
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep investing in services and infrastructure, even if taxes rise more

tradeoffs.context: Each budget weighs what residents pay this year against the services and repairs the District can afford now and later.

gains: Households and businesses may face smaller yearly tax bills
Spending decisions may get closer scrutiny
costs: Some repairs, facilities, or services may be delayed
Deferred upkeep can cost more when it is eventually done

gains: Aging facilities and infrastructure may be renewed sooner
Service levels may be kept or expanded as the population grows
costs: Property taxes and fees may rise faster than inflation
Higher costs may pass through to renters and small businesses

issues.title: Wastewater plant costs and Metro Vancouver
issues.description: How the District responds to the rising cost of the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant, which is billed to North Shore residents through Metro Vancouver.
issues.whatItAffects: Utility bills and property taxes for District households and businesses, and the District's relationship with the region.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets local utility rates, appoints its Metro Vancouver board representative, and can pass resolutions, seek inquiries, or advocate for how regional costs are shared.

viewQuestion.question: How should the District respond to wastewater plant costs?
viewQuestion.poleA: Press for an independent inquiry and pursue legal or rate challenges
viewQuestion.poleB: Work through Metro Vancouver to share costs and reform its governance

tradeoffs.context: The District can push hard against the region on these costs or negotiate within Metro Vancouver, and each path has risks.

gains: Residents may learn more about how costs grew
Pressure may improve the odds of cost relief for North Shore payers
costs: Inquiries and legal action take time and money with uncertain results
Tension with regional partners may affect other shared projects

gains: Cost-sharing and governance changes could apply to future regional projects
The District keeps working relationships with other municipalities
costs: Relief for current North Shore bills may be smaller or slower
Some residents may feel past decisions go unexamined

issues.title: Affordable, rental, and supportive housing
issues.description: Whether and how the District uses its land, fees, and approvals to add below-market rental, social, and supportive housing, and how sites are chosen.
issues.whatItAffects: Lower-income renters, seniors, local workers, people who are unhoused, and neighbours of proposed sites.
issues.whoDecides: Council can provide District-owned land, direct developer contributions to housing funds, set rental and non-market requirements, and approve sites in partnership with BC Housing.

viewQuestion.question: How should the District approach below-market and supportive housing?
viewQuestion.poleA: Use more District land and funds to add these homes across the community
viewQuestion.poleB: Add them more selectively, with stronger neighbourhood input on sites

tradeoffs.context: The District can move faster on below-market housing or spend more time on site selection and neighbourhood agreement.

gains: More people with low or moderate incomes may find homes in the District
Local workers may live closer to their jobs
costs: District land and funds used here are not available for other uses
Some neighbours may object to sites chosen with less consultation

gains: Neighbours may have more say in where projects go
Projects may face less opposition once approved
costs: Fewer below-market homes may be built in the near term
Longer processes may raise costs for housing partners

issues.title: Natural areas, climate, and wildfire
issues.description: How the District protects forests and habitat, prepares for wildfire, drought, and storms, and weighs climate goals in its decisions.
issues.whatItAffects: Residents near forested areas, parks and trail users, wildlife, and the District's infrastructure costs.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets land-use designations, park dedications, tree and environmental bylaws, wildfire mitigation work, and climate action spending.

viewQuestion.question: How should the District weigh nature protection against other needs?
viewQuestion.poleA: Protect more forest and habitat, and expand climate and wildfire work
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep current protections and focus spending on core services

tradeoffs.context: Protecting more land and expanding climate work uses land and budget that could go to other priorities.

gains: More forest, habitat, and trails may be kept for the long term
Risks from wildfire and extreme weather may be reduced
costs: Less land may be available for housing or other uses
Added programs may add to District budgets

gains: More budget may stay available for roads, facilities, and services
More flexibility may remain for future land-use decisions
costs: Some natural areas may face future development pressure
Climate and wildfire risks may grow without added work

issues.title: Recreation facilities, amenities, and childcare
issues.description: How quickly the District renews aging recreation centres and adds parks, sports facilities, gathering places, and childcare spaces.
issues.whatItAffects: Families, youth, seniors, sports groups, and neighbourhoods expecting amenities as they grow.
issues.whoDecides: Council decides capital spending on facilities and parks, uses amenity contributions from development, and can ease permitting or partner on childcare spaces.

viewQuestion.question: How should the District approach facilities and amenities?
viewQuestion.poleA: Build and renew facilities sooner, including through borrowing
viewQuestion.poleB: Phase projects over time to limit cost and borrowing

tradeoffs.context: Facility projects are large, so timing affects both service levels and the District's budget.

gains: Residents may get updated facilities and more spaces sooner
Construction costs may be locked in before they rise further
costs: Borrowing and debt payments may add to taxes
Other capital projects may need to wait

gains: Spending may be spread out with less pressure on taxes
Projects can be adjusted as needs and costs become clearer
costs: Aging facilities may face higher repair costs or closures
Waitlists for programs and childcare may persist longer

issues.title: Amalgamation with the City of North Vancouver
issues.description: Whether the District and the City of North Vancouver should move toward merging or sharing more services.
issues.whatItAffects: How the North Shore is governed, local representation, and the cost of services in both municipalities.
issues.whoDecides: Council can study amalgamation, place a non-binding question on a future ballot, and negotiate shared services with the City; a merger also requires provincial approval.

viewQuestion.question: What should the District do about amalgamation?
viewQuestion.poleA: Hold a public vote on merging with the City
viewQuestion.poleB: Stay separate and cooperate on specific services

tradeoffs.context: Merging could simplify governance but would change representation and require a costly transition.

gains: One government may reduce duplication and simplify planning
Residents would have a direct say through a vote
costs: A merger process may be costly and take years
Some residents may feel their area has less local representation

gains: Each municipality keeps its own council, finances, and local priorities
Avoids the cost and disruption of a transition
costs: Some duplication of staff and services may continue
Coordinating across two governments may remain slower

election.name: District of North Vancouver general local election
election.howToVote: Eligible electors who are not already on the voters list can register at the voting place when they vote. To register there, you show two pieces of identification that together prove your identity and residential address, and one must include your signature, such as a driver's licence. Non-resident property electors must also show proof of their right to register for the property and, where applicable, written consent from a majority of the property's owners. Advance voting is held before general voting day, including at District Hall (355 West Queens Road), and there are more than 20 voting places on October 17; check the District's election page for advance voting dates and hours and your voting place.
election.voteByMail: The District's election bylaw allows mail ballot voting; a mail ballot must be received by the Chief Election Officer before voting closes on general voting day. Application details are on the District's election page.

notes: Candidate list (5 mayor, 15 council for 6 seats) is from the District's declaration of candidates PDF and matches localelections.ca. No elector organizations appear on either list; every candidate runs without an affiliation, so electorOrganizations is empty. Election logistics: dnv.org election pages (2026-general-local-election, information-for-voters, see-who-is-running) load their content by script and returned no text; North Shore News pages returned 403 and thenorthshorelocal.com was unreachable (robots.txt timeout). Advance voting dates and hours could not be confirmed, so advanceVoting is left empty; howToVote cites the North Shore Daily Post for District Hall (355 West Queens Road) as an advance voting place and 20+ voting places on October 17. Mail ballot text comes from the District's election bylaw (Bylaw 6876), not a 2026 notice, so application deadlines are not given. Candidates with no positions: Paolo Pucci (no campaign website found; a change.org advocacy update characterizing his stance was not used), Max Zahedi (maxformayor.ca blocked by robots.txt fetch failure), and Daina Boyd (dainaboyd.ca loads by script; her North Shore Daily Post announcement was blocked by robots.txt fetch failure). The North Shore News 2026 candidate Q&A, likely the best source for these three, returned 403. Betty Forbes's and Lisa Muri's campaign sites were unreadable (script-loaded / robots-disallowed), so their entries use a North Vancouver District Public Library board bio (Forbes), the 2022 North Vancouver Chamber candidate Q&A (Muri, Hanson), October 2025 North Shore Daily Post council-vote coverage, and a Globe and Mail article (updated February 2025) for Muri; older statements are dated in the summaries. Jim Hanson's 2026 positions come from his campaign site. Hanson has proposed a fireworks-ban question for the 2026 ballot (North Shore Daily Post headline), but no official ballot question could be confirmed, so ballotQuestions is empty. csdId 5915046 was carried over and not re-verified in this pass.
